questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An electron is projected horizontally with a kinetic energy of $10 \text{ keV}$. A magnetic field of magnitude $1.0 \times 10^{-7} \text{ T}$ is present in the vertically upward direction. Calculate the lateral deflection of the electron after it has travelled a distance of $1 \text{ m}$. Employ suitable approximations.
questions.solution:
Kinetic energy of the electron, $K = 10 \text{ keV} = 10 \times 10^3 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J} = 1.6 \times 10^{-15} \text{ J}$

The radius of the circular path described by the electron in the magnetic field is given by:

$R = \dfrac{mv}{qB} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mK}}{qB}$

Substituting the given values:

$R = \dfrac{\sqrt{2 \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-15}}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.0 \times 10^{-7}}$

$R = \dfrac{\sqrt{29.12 \times 10^{-46}}}{1.6 \times 10^{-26}} = \dfrac{5.396 \times 10^{-23}}{1.6 \times 10^{-26}} \approx 3372.5 \text{ m}$

Since the distance travelled $x = 1 \text{ m}$ is much smaller than the radius $R$, the lateral deflection $y$ can be approximated using the relation $y \approx \dfrac{x^2}{2R}$:

$y \approx \dfrac{1^2}{2 \times 3372.5} \approx 1.48 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}$

$y \approx 0.0148 \text{ cm} \approx 0.015 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a region where a $1.0 \text{ T}$ magnetic field points from south to north, an alpha particle is projected vertically upward at a speed of $3.0 \times 10^4 \text{ km s}^{-1}$. Determine the magnetic force acting on the $\alpha$-particle.
questions.solution:
Charge of an alpha particle, $q = +2e = 3.2 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$

Velocity, $v = 3.0 \times 10^4 \text{ km s}^{-1} = 3.0 \times 10^7 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Magnetic field, $B = 1.0 \text{ T}$

Let East be $\hat{i}$, North be $\hat{j}$, and vertically upward be $\hat{k}$.

$\vec{v} = 3.0 \times 10^7 \hat{k} \text{ m s}^{-1}$

$\vec{B} = 1.0 \hat{j} \text{ T}$

Magnetic force, $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$

$\vec{F} = 3.2 \times 10^{-19} (3.0 \times 10^7 \hat{k} \times 1.0 \hat{j})$

$\vec{F} = 9.6 \times 10^{-12} (\hat{k} \times \hat{j}) \text{ N}$

Since $\hat{k} \times \hat{j} = -\hat{i}$, the force is directed towards the west.

Magnitude of force is $9.6 \times 10^{-12} \text{ N}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle carrying a charge of $1.0 \times 10^{-9} \text{ C}$ travels in the $x$–$y$ plane. A magnetic field of $4.0 \times 10^{-3} \vec{k} \text{ T}$ exerts a force of $(4.0 \vec{i} + 3.0 \vec{j}) \times 10^{-10} \text{ N}$ on it. Determine the velocity of the particle.
questions.solution:
The magnetic force on a moving charge is given by $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$.

Since the particle travels in the $x$-$y$ plane, its velocity can be written as $\vec{v} = v_x \hat{i} + v_y \hat{j}$.

Substituting the given values into the force equation:

$\vec{F} = 1.0 \times 10^{-9} [ (v_x \hat{i} + v_y \hat{j}) \times (4.0 \times 10^{-3} \hat{k}) ]$

$\vec{F} = 4.0 \times 10^{-12} [ v_x (\hat{i} \times \hat{k}) + v_y (\hat{j} \times \hat{k}) ]$

Using the cross product rules $\hat{i} \times \hat{k} = -\hat{j}$ and $\hat{j} \times \hat{k} = \hat{i}$:

$\vec{F} = 4.0 \times 10^{-12} (v_y \hat{i} - v_x \hat{j}) \text{ N}$

Equating this to the given force $\vec{F} = (4.0 \hat{i} + 3.0 \hat{j}) \times 10^{-10} \text{ N}$:

$4.0 \times 10^{-12} v_y = 4.0 \times 10^{-10} \Rightarrow v_y = 100 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

$-4.0 \times 10^{-12} v_x = 3.0 \times 10^{-10} \Rightarrow v_x = -75 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Therefore, the velocity of the particle is $\vec{v} = (-75 \hat{i} + 100 \hat{j}) \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An experimenter's logbook contains the following entry: "a charged particle is projected in a magnetic field of $(7.0 \vec{i} - 3.0 \vec{j}) \times 10^{-3} \text{ T}$. The acceleration of the particle is determined to be $(\Box \vec{i} + 7.0 \vec{j}) \times 10^{-6} \text{ m s}^{-2}$". The number to the left of $\vec{i}$ in the latter expression is illegible. What could this number be?
questions.solution:
The magnetic force on a moving charged particle is given by $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$.

Since the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the magnetic field, the acceleration $\vec{a}$ of the particle must also be perpendicular to $\vec{B}$.

Therefore, the dot product of acceleration and magnetic field must be zero, $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{B} = 0$.

Given $\vec{B} = (7.0 \hat{i} - 3.0 \hat{j}) \times 10^{-3} \text{ T}$ and $\vec{a} = (x \hat{i} + 7.0 \hat{j}) \times 10^{-6} \text{ m s}^{-2}$.

Taking the dot product:

$(x \hat{i} + 7.0 \hat{j}) \cdot (7.0 \hat{i} - 3.0 \hat{j}) = 0$

$7.0x - 21.0 = 0$

$x = 3.0$

The missing number is $3.0$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A $10 \text{ g}$ bullet carrying a charge of $4.00 \mu\text{C}$ is fired horizontally at a speed of $270 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. A vertical magnetic field of $500 \mu\text{T}$ is present in the region. Determine the deflection of the bullet caused by the magnetic field over a travel distance of $100 \text{ m}$. Use appropriate approximations.
questions.solution:
The magnetic force acting on the bullet is perpendicular to its velocity and is given by $F = qvB$.

The acceleration of the bullet due to this magnetic force is $a = \dfrac{F}{m} = \dfrac{qvB}{m}$.

Since the deflection is very small, the horizontal velocity remains approximately constant. The time taken to travel a horizontal distance $x$ is $t = \dfrac{x}{v}$.

The deflection $y$ caused by the magnetic field is given by the second equation of motion:

$y = \dfrac{1}{2}at^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\dfrac{qvB}{m}\right) \left(\dfrac{x}{v}\right)^2 = \dfrac{qBx^2}{2mv}$

Substituting the given values:
$q = 4.00 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$
$B = 500 \times 10^{-6} \text{ T} = 5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ T}$
$x = 100 \text{ m}$
$m = 10 \text{ g} = 10^{-2} \text{ kg}$
$v = 270 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

$y = \dfrac{4 \times 10^{-6} \times 5 \times 10^{-4} \times (100)^2}{2 \times 10^{-2} \times 270}$

$y = \dfrac{20 \times 10^{-10} \times 10^4}{5.4 \times 10^{-2} \times 10^2} = \dfrac{20 \times 10^{-6}}{5.4}$

$y = \dfrac{200}{54} \times 10^{-6} \approx 3.7 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A proton released from rest in a room experiences an initial acceleration $a_0$ directed towards the west. If, instead, it is projected towards the north at a speed $v_0$, its initial acceleration becomes $3 a_0$ towards the west. Determine the electric field and the minimum possible magnetic field present in the room.
options: Electric field is $\dfrac{m a_0}{e}$ towards west, and minimum magnetic field is $\dfrac{4 m a_0}{e v_0}$ downward
Electric field is $\dfrac{3 m a_0}{e}$ towards west, and minimum magnetic field is $\dfrac{2 m a_0}{e v_0}$ downward
Electric field is $\dfrac{m a_0}{e}$ towards east, and minimum magnetic field is $\dfrac{2 m a_0}{e v_0}$ upward
Electric field is $\dfrac{m a_0}{e}$ towards west, and minimum magnetic field is $\dfrac{2 m a_0}{e v_0}$ downward
questions.solution:
Let the directions be represented by unit vectors: East as $\hat{i}$, West as $-\hat{i}$, North as $\hat{j}$, South as $-\hat{j}$, Upward as $\hat{k}$, and Downward as $-\hat{k}$.

When the proton is released from rest, its velocity $\vec{v} = 0$. The only force acting on it is due to the electric field $\vec{E}$.

$\vec{F}_e = e\vec{E} = m\vec{a}$

$e\vec{E} = m(a_0(-\hat{i})) \Rightarrow \vec{E} = \dfrac{ma_0}{e}(-\hat{i})$

Thus, the electric field is $\dfrac{ma_0}{e}$ towards the west.

When the proton is projected towards the north with speed $v_0$, its velocity is $\vec{v} = v_0\hat{j}$. The total force is the vector sum of the electric and magnetic forces.

$\vec{F}_{total} = e\vec{E} + e(\vec{v} \times \vec{B}) = m\vec{a}'$

Given that the new acceleration is $3a_0$ towards the west, we have:

$-ma_0\hat{i} + e(v_0\hat{j} \times \vec{B}) = m(3a_0(-\hat{i}))$

$e(v_0\hat{j} \times \vec{B}) = -2ma_0\hat{i}$

Let the magnetic field be $\vec{B} = B_x\hat{i} + B_y\hat{j} + B_z\hat{k}$. Substituting this into the cross product:

$ev_0\hat{j} \times (B_x\hat{i} + B_y\hat{j} + B_z\hat{k}) = -2ma_0\hat{i}$

$ev_0(-B_x\hat{k} + B_z\hat{i}) = -2ma_0\hat{i}$

Comparing the components on both sides:

$ev_0B_z = -2ma_0 \Rightarrow B_z = -\dfrac{2ma_0}{ev_0}$

$-ev_0B_x = 0 \Rightarrow B_x = 0$

The component $B_y$ does not contribute to the magnetic force and can be any real number. However, to find the minimum possible magnitude of the magnetic field $|\vec{B}| = \sqrt{B_x^2 + B_y^2 + B_z^2}$, we must set $B_y = 0$.

Therefore, the minimum magnetic field is:

$\vec{B} = -\dfrac{2ma_0}{ev_0}\hat{k}$

Since $\hat{k}$ represents the upward direction, $-\hat{k}$ represents the downward direction. Thus, the minimum magnetic field is $\dfrac{2ma_0}{ev_0}$ downward.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A $10$-cm long portion of a straight wire carrying a $10 \text{ A}$ current is situated in a $0.1 \text{ T}$ magnetic field that is oriented at an angle of $53^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$ relative to the wire. What magnetic force acts on this portion of the wire?
options: $0.08 \text{ N}$ perpendicular to both the wire and the field
$0.08 \text{ N}$ parallel to the magnetic field
$0.06 \text{ N}$ perpendicular to both the wire and the field
$0.10 \text{ N}$ perpendicular to both the wire and the field
questions.solution:
The magnetic force on a current-carrying wire is given by the formula:

$\vec{F} = I(\vec{L} \times \vec{B})$

The magnitude of the force is:

$F = I L B \sin\theta$

Given values are:

$I = 10 \text{ A}$

$L = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$

$B = 0.1 \text{ T}$

$\theta = 53^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$

Substituting these values into the formula:

$F = 10 \times 0.1 \times 0.1 \times \sin(53^{}^{{}^{\circ}})$

$F = 0.1 \times \dfrac{4}{5} = 0.08 \text{ N}$

From the cross product $\vec{L} \times \vec{B}$, the direction of the magnetic force is perpendicular to both the wire and the magnetic field.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An electron is projected horizontally with a kinetic energy of $10 \text{ keV}$. A magnetic field of magnitude $1.0 \times 10^{-7} \text{ T}$ is present in the vertically upward direction. Will the electron deflect to the left or to the right of its original direction of motion?
questions.solution:
Let the direction of motion of the electron be along the $+x$-axis, so $\vec{v} = v \hat{i}$.

Let the vertically upward direction be along the $+y$-axis, so $\vec{B} = B \hat{j}$.

The magnetic force experienced by a moving charge is given by $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$.

For an electron, $q = -e$. Substituting the values, we get:

$\vec{F} = -e(v \hat{i} \times B \hat{j}) = -evB(\hat{i} \times \hat{j}) = -evB \hat{k}$

In a right-handed coordinate system, if $+x$ is forward and $+y$ is upward, the $+z$-axis ($\hat{k}$) points to the left.

Since the force is in the $-\hat{k}$ direction, the electron will deflect towards the right.

questions.q: A $2 \text{ A}$ current enters at the corner $d$ of a square frame $abcd$ having a side length of $20 \text{ cm}$ and exits at the opposite corner $b$. A magnetic field $B = 0.1 \text{ T}$ is present in the region, directed perpendicular to the plane of the frame as shown in the figure. Determine the magnitude and direction of the magnetic forces acting on the four sides of the frame.
options: $0.04 \text{ N}$ on each wire; on $da$ and $cb$ towards right, and on $dc$ and $ab$ upward
$0.02 \text{ N}$ on each wire; on $da$ and $cb$ towards left, and on $dc$ and $ab$ downward
$0.04 \text{ N}$ on each wire; on $da$ and $cb$ towards left, and on $dc$ and $ab$ downward
$0.02 \text{ N}$ on each wire; on $da$ and $cb$ towards right, and on $dc$ and $ab$ upward
questions.solution:
The total current entering the square frame at corner $d$ is $I = 2 \text{ A}$.

Since the frame is a square made of uniform wire, the resistance of the path $d \to a \to b$ is equal to the resistance of the path $d \to c \to b$. Therefore, the current splits equally into the two branches.

Current in each side of the frame is:
$I_{da} = I_{ab} = I_{dc} = I_{cb} = \dfrac{2}{2} = 1 \text{ A}$

The magnetic field is uniform, directed perpendicular to the plane of the frame and outwards (indicated by dots), so $\vec{B} = 0.1 \hat{k} \text{ T}$.

The magnitude of the magnetic force on each wire of length $L = 20 \text{ cm} = 0.2 \text{ m}$ is given by:
$F = I L B \sin(90^{\circ}) = 1 \times 0.2 \times 0.1 = 0.02 \text{ N}$

The direction of the force on each wire can be found using $\vec{F} = I(\vec{L} \times \vec{B})$:
For wire $da$: Current is downwards ($-\hat{j}$). $\vec{F}_{da} = 1(-0.2\hat{j} \times 0.1\hat{k}) = -0.02\hat{i} \text{ N}$ (towards left).
For wire $cb$: Current is downwards ($-\hat{j}$). $\vec{F}_{cb} = 1(-0.2\hat{j} \times 0.1\hat{k}) = -0.02\hat{i} \text{ N}$ (towards left).
For wire $dc$: Current is rightwards ($\hat{i}$). $\vec{F}_{dc} = 1(0.2\hat{i} \times 0.1\hat{k}) = -0.02\hat{j} \text{ N}$ (downward).
For wire $ab$: Current is rightwards ($\hat{i}$). $\vec{F}_{ab} = 1(0.2\hat{i} \times 0.1\hat{k}) = -0.02\hat{j} \text{ N}$ (downward).

Thus, the force is $0.02 \text{ N}$ on each wire; on $da$ and $cb$ towards left, and on $dc$ and $ab$ downward.

questions.q: As shown in the figure, a strong electromagnet produces a magnetic field of strength $1.0 \text{ T}$ inside a cylindrical region of radius $4.0 \text{ cm}$. A wire carrying a current of $2.0 \text{ A}$ is positioned perpendicular to and intersecting the axis of the cylindrical region. Determine the magnitude of the force exerted on the wire.
questions.solution:
Given parameters are magnetic field $B = 1.0 \text{ T}$, radius of the cylindrical region $r = 4.0 \text{ cm} = 0.04 \text{ m}$, and current $i = 2.0 \text{ A}$.

Since the wire intersects the axis of the cylindrical region, the length of the wire inside the magnetic field is equal to the diameter of the cylinder.

Effective length of the wire in the magnetic field is $l = 2r = 2 \times 0.04 = 0.08 \text{ m}$.

The magnetic force on the current-carrying wire is given by $F = i l B \sin\theta$.

As the wire is perpendicular to the magnetic field, $\theta = 90^{\circ}$.

Substituting the values, we get:

$F = 2.0 \times 0.08 \times 1.0 \times \sin 90^{\circ}$

$F = 0.16 \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wire having length $l$ carries a current $i$ directed along the $x$-axis. A magnetic field is present and is described by $\vec{B} = B_0 (\vec{i} + \vec{j} + \vec{k}) \text{ T}$. Determine the magnitude of the magnetic force acting on the wire.
questions.solution:
The magnetic force acting on a current-carrying wire is given by $\vec{F} = i(\vec{l} \times \vec{B})$.

Since the wire is directed along the $x$-axis, the length vector is $\vec{l} = l \hat{i}$.

The magnetic field is given as $\vec{B} = B_0 (\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k})$.

Substituting these into the force formula:

$\vec{F} = i (l \hat{i} \times B_0 (\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}))$

$\vec{F} = i l B_0 (\hat{i} \times \hat{i} + \hat{i} \times \hat{j} + \hat{i} \times \hat{k})$

Using the properties of cross products, $\hat{i} \times \hat{i} = 0$, $\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}$, and $\hat{i} \times \hat{k} = -\hat{j}$, we get:

$\vec{F} = i l B_0 (\hat{k} - \hat{j})$

The magnitude of the magnetic force is:

$|\vec{F}| = i l B_0 \sqrt{(-1)^2 + (1)^2} = \sqrt{2} B_0 i l$

questions.q: In the circuit depicted in the figure, a current of $5.0 \text{ A}$ is present. The wire $PQ$ measures $50 \text{ cm}$ in length and is immersed in a magnetic field with a magnitude of $0.20 \text{ T}$. Determine the magnetic force exerted on the wire $PQ$.
options: $50 \text{ N}$ towards the inside of the circuit
$0.50 \text{ N}$ towards the outside of the circuit
$50 \text{ N}$ towards the outside of the circuit
$0.50 \text{ N}$ towards the inside of the circuit
questions.solution:
Given:
Current, $I = 5.0 \text{ A}$
Length of wire PQ, $L = 50 \text{ cm} = 0.5 \text{ m}$
Magnetic field, $B = 0.20 \text{ T}$

The magnitude of the magnetic force on the current-carrying wire is given by:
$F = ILB \sin\theta$

Since the magnetic field is perpendicular to the plane of the circuit, $\theta = 90^\circ$.
$F = 5.0 \times 0.5 \times 0.20 = 0.50 \text{ N}$

In the given circuit diagram, the longer line of the battery symbol represents the positive terminal, so the current flows in a clockwise direction. Therefore, the current in wire PQ flows from P to Q (towards the right).

The magnetic field is directed into the plane of the paper. Using the right-hand rule for the cross product $\vec{F} = I(\vec{L} \times \vec{B})$ (or Fleming's Left-Hand Rule), with the current vector $\vec{L}$ pointing right and the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ pointing into the page, the resulting magnetic force is directed upwards.

An upward force on wire PQ points towards the inside of the closed circuit loop.

Thus, the magnetic force is $0.50 \text{ N}$ towards the inside of the circuit.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A circular loop of radius $a$, carrying a current $i$, is situated in a two-dimensional magnetic field. The centre of the loop coincides with the centre of the field. The strength of the magnetic field at the periphery of the loop is $B$. Determine the magnetic force on the wire.
options: $\pi a^2 i B$, directed into the plane of the figure
$2\pi a i B$, directed out of the plane of the figure
$2\pi a i B$, directed into the plane of the figure
questions.solution:
Consider a small current element $d\vec{l}$ on the circular loop.

The magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is radial and points outwards from the centre. The current element $d\vec{l}$ is tangential to the circular loop.

The angle between the current element $d\vec{l}$ and the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is $90^{\circ}$.

The magnetic force on this small element is given by $d\vec{F} = i(d\vec{l} \times \vec{B})$.

The magnitude of this force is $dF = i B dl \sin(90^{\circ}) = i B dl$.

Using the right-hand rule, the direction of the cross product $d\vec{l} \times \vec{B}$ is into the plane of the figure for all elements along the loop.

Since the force on every element is directed into the plane of the figure, the total magnetic force is the sum of the magnitudes of these elemental forces.

$F = \int dF = \int i B dl = i B \int dl$

The total length of the loop is $\int dl = 2\pi a$.

Therefore, $F = i B (2\pi a) = 2\pi a i B$.

The net force is $2\pi a i B$, directed into the plane of the figure.

Answer: $2\pi a i B$, directed into the plane of the figure

The total length of the loop is $\int dl = 2\pi a$.

questions.q: In a certain region, a hypothetical magnetic field is described by $\vec{B} = B_0 \vec{e_r}$, where $\vec{e_r}$ represents the unit vector in the radial direction. A circular loop of radius $a$ carrying a current $i$ is positioned such that its plane is parallel to the $x$-$y$ plane, with its centre located at $(0, 0, d)$. Determine the magnitude of the magnetic force exerted on the loop.
questions.solution:
The position vector of any point on the circular loop is given by:

$\vec{r} = a \cos\theta \hat{i} + a \sin\theta \hat{j} + d \hat{k}$

The distance of any point on the loop from the origin is:

$r = |\vec{r}| = \sqrt{a^2 + d^2}$

The unit vector in the radial direction is $\vec{e_r} = \dfrac{\vec{r}}{r}$. Thus, the magnetic field at the loop is:

$\vec{B} = B_0 \vec{e_r} = \dfrac{B_0}{\sqrt{a^2 + d^2}} (a \cos\theta \hat{i} + a \sin\theta \hat{j} + d \hat{k})$

The current element vector $d\vec{l}$ along the loop is:

$d\vec{l} = d\vec{r} = (-a \sin\theta \hat{i} + a \cos\theta \hat{j}) d\theta$

The magnetic force on this small current element is $d\vec{F} = i(d\vec{l} \times \vec{B})$.

Calculating the cross product:

$d\vec{l} \times \vec{B} = \dfrac{B_0 d\theta}{\sqrt{a^2 + d^2}} \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} \text{ and } \hat{j} \text{ and } \hat{k} \\ -a \sin\theta \text{ and } a \cos\theta \text{ and } 0 \\ a \cos\theta \text{ and } a \sin\theta \text{ and } d \end{vmatrix}$

$d\vec{l} \times \vec{B} = \dfrac{B_0 d\theta}{\sqrt{a^2 + d^2}} [ (a d \cos\theta) \hat{i} - (-a d \sin\theta) \hat{j} + (-a^2 \sin^2\theta - a^2 \cos^2\theta) \hat{k} ]$

$d\vec{l} \times \vec{B} = \dfrac{B_0 d\theta}{\sqrt{a^2 + d^2}} (a d \cos\theta \hat{i} + a d \sin\theta \hat{j} - a^2 \hat{k})$

The total force on the loop is obtained by integrating $d\vec{F}$ from $\theta = 0$ to $\theta = 2\pi$:

$\vec{F} = \int_{0}^{2\pi} \dfrac{i B_0}{\sqrt{a^2 + d^2}} (a d \cos\theta \hat{i} + a d \sin\theta \hat{j} - a^2 \hat{k}) d\theta$

Since $\int_{0}^{2\pi} \cos\theta d\theta = 0$ and $\int_{0}^{2\pi} \sin\theta d\theta = 0$, the $\hat{i}$ and $\hat{j}$ components vanish.

$\vec{F} = \dfrac{i B_0}{\sqrt{a^2 + d^2}} (-a^2 \hat{k}) \int_{0}^{2\pi} d\theta = -\dfrac{2\pi a^2 i B_0}{\sqrt{a^2 + d^2}} \hat{k}$

The magnitude of the magnetic force exerted on the loop is:

$|\vec{F}| = \dfrac{2\pi a^2 i B_0}{\sqrt{a^2 + d^2}}$

questions.q: A rectangular wire-loop of width $a$ is suspended from the insulated pan of a spring balance, as shown in the figure. A current $i$ flows in the anticlockwise direction through the loop. A magnetic field $B$ is present in the lower region. Determine the change in the tension of the spring when the current in the loop is reversed.
questions.solution:
Let $W$ be the weight of the rectangular wire-loop.

The magnetic field $B$ is present only in the lower region and is directed into the plane of the paper. The magnetic forces on the vertical segments of the loop are equal and opposite in the horizontal direction, cancelling each other out.

The net magnetic force acts on the bottom horizontal segment of width $a$.

When the current $i$ flows in the anticlockwise direction, the current in the bottom segment is directed towards the right. Using the magnetic force formula $\vec{F} = i(\vec{l} \times \vec{B})$, the force is directed upwards.

The magnitude of this upward magnetic force is $F_B = i a B$.

The initial tension in the spring balance is:

$T_1 = W - i a B$

When the current is reversed, it flows in the clockwise direction, and the current in the bottom segment is directed towards the left. The magnetic force is now directed downwards with the same magnitude.

The new tension in the spring balance becomes:

$T_2 = W + i a B$

The change in the tension of the spring is:

$\Delta T = T_2 - T_1$

$\Delta T = (W + i a B) - (W - i a B) = 2 i a B$

questions.q: A current loop of arbitrary shape is situated in a uniform magnetic field $B$. Determine the net magnetic force exerted on the loop.
options: Dependent on the shape of the loop
questions.solution:
The magnetic force on a small current element $d\vec{l}$ is given by $d\vec{F} = I(d\vec{l} \times \vec{B})$.

The net magnetic force on the closed loop is $\vec{F} = \oint d\vec{F} = \oint I(d\vec{l} \times \vec{B})$.

Since the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is uniform, it is constant over the loop and can be taken outside the integral.

$\vec{F} = I \left( \oint d\vec{l} \right) \times \vec{B}$

For any closed loop, the vector sum of the displacement elements is zero, i.e., $\oint d\vec{l} = 0$.

Thus, $\vec{F} = I(0) \times \vec{B} = 0$.

The net magnetic force on any closed current loop in a uniform magnetic field is always zero.

questions.q: A current-carrying wire joining two fixed points $a$ and $b$ is placed in a uniform magnetic field. The force acting on the wire is:
options: dependent on the total length of the wire.
independent of the shape of the wire.
dependent on the shape of the wire.
questions.solution:
The magnetic force on a small element $d\vec{l}$ of the wire carrying current $I$ in a magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is given by $d\vec{F} = I(d\vec{l} \times \vec{B})$.

The total force on the wire from point $a$ to point $b$ is obtained by integrating the force over the entire length of the wire:

$\vec{F} = \int_a^{b} I(d\vec{l} \times \vec{B})$

Since the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is uniform, it is constant and can be taken out of the integral:

$\vec{F} = I \left( \int_a^{b} d\vec{l} \right) \times \vec{B}$

The integral $\int_a^{b} d\vec{l}$ is simply the displacement vector $\vec{L}$ from the initial point $a$ to the final point $b$.

$\vec{F} = I(\vec{L} \times \vec{B})$

This expression shows that the net magnetic force depends only on the displacement vector between the two fixed points $a$ and $b$, the current $I$, and the uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$. It does not depend on the actual path taken by the wire between these two points. Thus, the force is independent of the shape of the wire.

questions.q: A current of $5.0 \text{ A}$ flows in a semicircular wire having a radius of $5.0 \text{ cm}$. A magnetic field $B$ with a magnitude of $0.50 \text{ T}$ is present perpendicular to the plane of the wire. Determine the magnitude of the magnetic force exerted on this wire.
questions.solution:
The magnetic force on a current-carrying wire in a uniform magnetic field is given by $\vec{F} = I(\vec{L} \times \vec{B})$, where $\vec{L}$ is the displacement vector from the initial point to the final point of the wire.

For a semicircular wire of radius $R$, the magnitude of the displacement vector is the diameter of the semicircle, so $L = 2R$.

Since the magnetic field is perpendicular to the plane of the wire, the angle between $\vec{L}$ and $\vec{B}$ is $90^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}$.

The magnitude of the magnetic force is $F = I L B \sin(90^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}) = I(2R)B$.

Given $I = 5.0 \text{ A}$, $R = 5.0 \text{ cm} = 0.05 \text{ m}$, and $B = 0.50 \text{ T}$.

Substituting the values:

$F = 5.0 \times (2 \times 0.05) \times 0.50$

$F = 5.0 \times 0.10 \times 0.50 = 0.25 \text{ N}$

questions.q: A wire carrying a current $i$ is positioned in the $x$–$y$ plane along the curve $y = A \sin  \left(\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}x\right)$. A magnetic field $B$ is present in the $z$-direction. Determine the magnitude of the magnetic force acting on the section of the wire between $x = 0$ and $x = \lambda$.$
questions.solution:
The magnetic force on a current-carrying wire in a uniform magnetic field is given by $\vec{F} = \int i (d\vec{l} \times \vec{B})$.

Since the magnetic field $\vec{B} = B \hat{k}$ is uniform, the total force depends only on the displacement vector $\vec{L}$ between the initial and final points of the wire.

The initial point at $x = 0$ is $(0, 0, 0)$.

The final point at $x = \lambda$ is $(\lambda, A \sin(2\pi), 0) = (\lambda, 0, 0)$.

The displacement vector is $\vec{L} = \lambda \hat{i}$.

The magnetic force is $\vec{F} = i (\vec{L} \times \vec{B}) = i (\lambda \hat{i} \times B \hat{k}) = -i \lambda B \hat{j}$.

The magnitude of the magnetic force is $|\vec{F}| = i \lambda B$.

questions.q: A rigid wire consists of a semicircular portion of radius $R$ and two straight sections. The wire is partially immersed in a perpendicular magnetic field $B$ as shown in the figure. Determine the magnetic force on the wire if it carries a current $i$.
options: $2 i R B$, upward in the figure
$2 i R B$, downward in the figure
$\pi i R B$, upward in the figure
questions.solution:
The magnetic force on a current-carrying wire in a uniform magnetic field is given by $\vec{F} = i(\vec{L}_{eff} \times \vec{B})$, where $\vec{L}_{eff}$ is the displacement vector from the initial point to the final point of the wire in the magnetic field.

The wire consists of two vertical straight sections and a semicircular section. The straight sections carry current in opposite directions (one upwards, one downwards). The magnetic forces on these straight sections are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction (pointing horizontally outwards), thus cancelling each other out.

For the semicircular portion, the effective length is the straight-line distance between its ends, which is the diameter $2R$. The direction of $\vec{L}_{eff}$ is horizontally from left to right.

The magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is uniform and directed into the plane of the paper.

The magnitude of the net force is $F = i|\vec{L}_{eff}||\vec{B}|\sin(90^{\circ}) = i(2R)B = 2iRB$.

Using the right-hand rule for the cross product $\vec{L}_{eff} \times \vec{B}$, the direction of the force is upwards in the plane of the figure.

Therefore, the net magnetic force on the wire is $2iRB$, upward.

questions.q: A straight horizontal wire carrying a current of $2.0 ext{ A}$ has a mass of $10 ext{ mg}$ and a length of $1.0 ext{ m}$. Determine the minimum magnetic field $B$ that must be applied in the region in order for the magnetic force on the wire to balance its weight.
questions.solution:
For the magnetic force to balance the weight of the wire, the magnetic force must act upwards and its magnitude must be equal to the gravitational force.

The magnetic force on a current-carrying wire is given by $F_{m} = I L B \sin\theta$.

For the minimum magnetic field, $\theta = 90^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}$, so $\sin\theta = 1$.

Equating the magnetic force to the weight of the wire:

$I L B = m g$

Given:

$I = 2.0 \text{ A}$

$m = 10 \text{ mg} = 10 \times 10^{-6} \text{ kg} = 10^{-5} \text{ kg}$

$L = 1.0 \text{ m}$

$g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^{2}$

Substituting the values:

$2.0 \times 1.0 \times B = 10^{-5} \times 9.8$

$B = \dfrac{9.8 \times 10^{-5}}{2.0}$

$B = 4.9 \times 10^{-5} \text{ T}$

questions.q: As shown in the figure, a rod $PQ$ of length $20.0 \text{ cm}$ and mass $200 \text{ g}$ is suspended horizontally from a fixed point $O$ by two threads attached to its ends, each measuring $20.0 \text{ cm}$ in length. A uniform magnetic field of strength $0.500 \text{ T}$ is present in the region around the wire $PQ$, pointing out of the page. The connecting wires between $PQ$ and the battery are slack and do not exert any force on $PQ$. Determine the tension in each thread when the switch $S$ remains open.
questions.solution:
When the switch $S$ is open, no current flows through the rod $PQ$. Therefore, the magnetic force acting on the rod is zero.

The rod is in equilibrium under the action of its weight and the tensions in the two threads.

Given that the length of the rod $PQ = 20.0 \text{ cm}$ and the lengths of the threads $OP = OQ = 20.0 \text{ cm}$, $\triangle OPQ$ is an equilateral triangle.

The angle each thread makes with the horizontal rod is $60^\circ$.

Let $T$ be the tension in each thread. Balancing the forces in the vertical direction:

$2T \sin(60^\circ) = mg$

Substituting $m = 0.2 \text{ kg}$ and $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$2T \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 0.2 \times 9.8$

$T \sqrt{3} = 1.96$

$T = \dfrac{1.96}{\sqrt{3}} \approx 1.13 \text{ N}$

questions.q: Two metal strips, each of length $l$, are clamped parallel to one another on a horizontal floor with a separation $b$ between them. A wire of mass $m$ lies perpendicularly across them, as shown in the figure. A vertically upward magnetic field of strength $B$ is present in the space. The metal strips are smooth, whereas the coefficient of friction between the wire and the floor is $\mu$. Once the switch $S$ is closed at the instant $t = 0$, a current $i$ is established. Determine how far away from the strips the wire will reach before coming to a halt.
options: $\dfrac{2 i l b B}{\mu m g}$
questions.solution:
While the wire is on the metal strips, it experiences a magnetic force due to the current flowing through it. The magnitude of this magnetic force is given by:

$F_m = i b B$

Since the metal strips are smooth, there is no frictional force acting on the wire during this part of the motion. The work done by the magnetic force as the wire moves along the entire length $l$ of the strips is converted into its kinetic energy:

$W_m = F_m \times l = i b B l$

Let $v$ be the velocity of the wire just as it leaves the metal strips. Its kinetic energy is:

$K = i b B l$

Once the wire leaves the strips, it moves on the horizontal floor where the magnetic force is no longer present (as the circuit is broken), but it experiences a kinetic frictional force. The frictional force is:

$f_k = \mu m g$

Let $x$ be the distance the wire travels on the floor before coming to a halt. The work done by friction will dissipate the entire kinetic energy of the wire. By the work-energy theorem:

$W_f = \Delta K$

$-f_k \times x = 0 - K$

$\mu m g x = i b B l$

Solving for $x$, we get the distance the wire reaches away from the strips:

$x = \dfrac{i l b B}{\mu m g}$

questions.q: A metal wire $PQ$ having a mass of $10\text{ g}$ rests on two horizontal metal rails separated by $4.90\text{ cm}$. A vertically downward magnetic field with a magnitude of $0.800\text{ T}$ is present in the space. As the resistance of the circuit is slowly decreased, it is found that the wire $PQ$ begins sliding on the rails once the resistance drops below $20.0\text{ }\Omega$. Determine the coefficient of friction.
questions.solution:
When the resistance drops to $20.0 \text{ }\Omega$, the current in the circuit is:

$I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{6}{20.0} = 0.3 \text{ A}$

The magnetic force acting on the wire $PQ$ is given by:

$F_{m} = I L B$

Substituting the given values ($L = 4.90 \text{ cm} = 4.90 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$, $B = 0.800 \text{ T}$):

$F_{m} = 0.3 \times (4.90 \times 10^{-2}) \times 0.800 = 0.01176 \text{ N}$

The normal force on the wire is equal to its weight (taking $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$):

$N = mg = (10 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg}) \times 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2 = 0.098 \text{ N}$

The wire begins to slide when the magnetic force equals the maximum static friction force:

$F_{m} = \mu N$

$\mu = \dfrac{F_{m}}{N} = \dfrac{0.01176}{0.098} = 0.12$

Therefore, the coefficient of friction is $0.12$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A straight wire of mass $m$ and length $l$ is able to slide on two parallel plastic rails positioned in a horizontal plane with a separation $d$. The coefficient of friction between the wire and the rails is $\mu$. If the wire carries a current $i$, determine the minimum magnetic field that must be present in the space to make the wire slide on the rails.
questions.solution:
Since the rails are made of plastic, they are non-conducting. Therefore, the current $i$ must flow through the entire length $l$ of the wire, not just the part between the rails.

Let the magnetic field $B$ be applied vertically to the horizontal plane. The magnetic force acting on the current-carrying wire is given by:
$F_m = i l B$

The normal reaction force on the wire due to its weight is:
$N = m g$

The maximum static frictional force opposing the motion of the wire is:
$f = \mu N = \mu m g$

For the wire to just start sliding on the rails, the magnetic force must be equal to or greater than the maximum static frictional force:
$F_m \ge f$

Substituting the expressions for $F_m$ and $f$:
$i l B \ge \mu m g$

Rearranging the inequality to solve for the minimum magnetic field $B$:
$B \ge \dfrac{\mu m g}{i l}$

Thus, the minimum magnetic field required to make the wire slide is $\dfrac{\mu m g}{i l}$.

questions.q: A circular wire-loop of radius $a$, carrying a current $i$, is placed in a perpendicular magnetic field $B$. Determine the force of compression in the wire.
questions.solution:
Consider a small element of the circular wire subtending an angle $d\theta$ at the center.

The length of this element is $dl = a d\theta$.

The magnetic force on this element is $dF = i(dl)B = i(a d\theta)B$.

By the right-hand rule for $d\vec{l} \times \vec{B}$, this force is directed radially inwards, causing a compressive force $T$ in the wire.

The compressive forces act tangentially at the ends of the small element. The radial component of these forces balances the inward magnetic force.

The net inward radial force due to compression is $2T \sin\left(\dfrac{d\theta}{2}\right)$.

For a small angle $d\theta$, $\sin\left(\dfrac{d\theta}{2}\right) \approx \dfrac{d\theta}{2}$.

Equating the forces for equilibrium:

$2T \left(\dfrac{d\theta}{2}\right) = i a B d\theta$

$T d\theta = i a B d\theta$

$T = i a B$

Alternatively, considering a semicircular portion of the wire, the total magnetic force is $F = i(2a)B = 2iaB$ directed towards the center. This is balanced by the compressive forces at the two ends, so $2T = 2iaB \Rightarrow T = iaB$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A circular wire-loop of radius $a$ and carrying a current $i$ is placed in a perpendicular magnetic field $B$, as shown in the figure. Assume the radius of the wire's cross section is $r$. Determine the increase in the radius of the loop when the magnetic field is switched off. The Young modulus of the wire's material is $Y$.
questions.solution:
Consider a small element of the circular wire-loop subtending an angle $d\theta$ at the center. The length of this element is $dl = a d\theta$.

The magnetic force acting on this small element is given by:
$dF = i dl B = i (a d\theta) B$

According to the right-hand rule (or Fleming's left-hand rule), since the current is counter-clockwise and the magnetic field is directed into the page, the magnetic force on each element is directed radially inward. This inward force compresses the loop.

To maintain equilibrium, a compressive force (tension) $T$ is developed in the wire. The outward radial component of this compressive force from the two ends of the element balances the inward magnetic force:
$2T \sin\left(\dfrac{d\theta}{2}\right) = dF$

Since $d\theta$ is very small, $\sin\left(\dfrac{d\theta}{2}\right) \approx \dfrac{d\theta}{2}$.
$2T \left(\dfrac{d\theta}{2}\right) = i a B d\theta$
$T = i a B$

The compressive stress $\sigma$ in the wire is the force per unit cross-sectional area:
$\sigma = \dfrac{T}{A} = \dfrac{i a B}{\pi r^2}$

The longitudinal strain $\epsilon$ in the wire is given by Hooke's law:
$\epsilon = \dfrac{\sigma}{Y} = \dfrac{i a B}{\pi r^2 Y}$

The strain is also equal to the fractional change in the circumference, which is the same as the fractional change in the radius:
$\epsilon = \dfrac{\Delta L}{L} = \dfrac{\Delta (2\pi a)}{2\pi a} = \dfrac{\Delta a}{a}$

Equating the two expressions for strain:
$\dfrac{\Delta a}{a} = \dfrac{i a B}{\pi r^2 Y}$

$\Delta a = \dfrac{i a^2 B}{\pi r^2 Y}$

When the magnetic field is switched off, the compressive force vanishes, and the loop expands back to its natural length. Therefore, the increase in the radius of the loop is $\dfrac{i a^2 B}{\pi r^2 Y}$.

questions.q: In a certain region, the magnetic field is specified by $\vec{B} = B_0 \left(1 + \dfrac{x}{l}\right) \vec{k}$. A square loop carrying a current $i$ and having an edge length $l$ is situated with its edges parallel to the $x$ and $y$ axes. Determine the magnitude of the net magnetic force experienced by the loop.
questions.solution:
Consider the square loop placed in the $xy$-plane with its vertices at $(x, y)$, $(x+l, y)$, $(x+l, y+l)$, and $(x, y+l)$.

The magnetic force on a current element is $d\vec{F} = i(d\vec{l} \times \vec{B})$.

For the two edges parallel to the $x$-axis, the current flows in opposite directions. Since the magnetic field $\vec{B} = B_0 \left(1 + \dfrac{x}{l}\right) \hat{k}$ depends only on $x$, the forces on these two edges are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, cancelling each other out.

For the edge at $x + l$ parallel to the $y$-axis, the force is:

$\vec{F}_1 = i(l\hat{j}) \times \left[B_0\left(1 + \dfrac{x+l}{l}\right)\hat{k}\right] = i l B_0\left(1 + \dfrac{x+l}{l}\right)\hat{i}$

For the edge at $x$ parallel to the $y$-axis, the current flows in the opposite direction, so the force is:

$\vec{F}_2 = i(-l\hat{j}) \times \left[B_0\left(1 + \dfrac{x}{l}\right)\hat{k}\right] = -i l B_0\left(1 + \dfrac{x}{l}\right)\hat{i}$

The net magnetic force on the loop is the sum of the forces on all edges:

$\vec{F}_{net} = \vec{F}_1 + \vec{F}_2 = i l B_0 \left(1 + \dfrac{x+l}{l} - 1 - \dfrac{x}{l}\right)\hat{i}$

$\vec{F}_{net} = i l B_0 \left(\dfrac{l}{l}\right)\hat{i} = i B_0 l \hat{i}$

The magnitude of the net magnetic force experienced by the loop is $i B_0 l$.

Answer: $i B_0 l$

questions.q: A conducting wire of length $l$, positioned perpendicular to a magnetic field $B$, travels with a velocity $v$. Determine the potential difference that is established across the ends of the wire.
questions.solution:
The motional electromotive force (EMF) induced in a straight conducting wire of length $l$ moving with velocity $v$ perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field $B$ is given by:

$E = (\vec{v} \times \vec{B}) \cdot \vec{l}$

Since the velocity $\vec{v}$, magnetic field $\vec{B}$, and the length of the wire $\vec{l}$ are mutually perpendicular, the magnitude of the induced EMF is:

$E = vBl$

This induced EMF is equal to the potential difference established across the ends of the wire.

Therefore, the potential difference is $lBv$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A conducting wire of length $l$, situated perpendicular to a magnetic field $B$, travels with a velocity $v$. As a result of the magnetic force, electrons accumulate at one end, which establishes an electric field within the wire. This redistribution halts once the electric force acting on the free electrons offsets the magnetic force. Determine the electric field established inside the wire once the redistribution ends.
questions.solution:
When the conducting wire moves in the magnetic field, the free electrons experience a magnetic Lorentz force.

The magnitude of the magnetic force on an electron of charge $e$ is given by:
$F_m = evB$

This force causes electrons to accumulate at one end of the wire, creating an electric field $E$ along its length. The electric field exerts an electric force on the electrons in the opposite direction, with magnitude:
$F_e = eE$

In the steady state, the redistribution of electrons stops when the electric force balances the magnetic force:
$F_e = F_m$

Substituting the expressions for the forces, we get:
$eE = evB$

$E = vB$

Alternatively, the motional emf developed across the ends of the wire is $\varepsilon = Bvl$. The uniform electric field $E$ is related to the potential difference by $E = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{l}$.

Therefore, $E = \dfrac{Bvl}{l} = vB$.

questions.q: A current $i$ is passed through a silver strip of width $d$ and area of cross section $A$. The number of free electrons per unit volume is $n$. A magnetic field $B$ exists perpendicular to the plane of the strip. What will be the potential difference developed across the width of the conductor due to the electron accumulation? (The appearance of a transverse emf, when a current-carrying wire is placed in a magnetic field, is called Hall effect.)
questions.solution:
The drift velocity of the free electrons is $v_d$.

The current $i$ flowing through the strip is given by:

$i = n e A v_d$

$\Rightarrow v_d = \dfrac{i}{n e A}$

When the magnetic field $B$ is applied perpendicular to the current, the electrons experience a magnetic force:

$F_m = e v_d B$

This force causes electrons to accumulate on one side of the strip, setting up a transverse electric field $E$. In the steady state, the electric force balances the magnetic force:

$e E = e v_d B$

$\Rightarrow E = v_d B$

The potential difference $V$ developed across the width $d$ of the conductor is:

$V = E d = v_d B d$

Substituting the value of $v_d$, we get:

$V = \left(\dfrac{i}{n e A}\right) B d = \dfrac{i B d}{A n e}$

questions.q: A particle with a mass of $2.0 \times 10^{-10} \text{ g}$ and a charge of $2.0 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C}$ is projected at a speed of $2.0 \times 10^3 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ into a region containing a uniform magnetic field of $0.10 \text{ T}$. The particle's velocity is perpendicular to the magnetic field. Determine the radius of the circular path described by the particle, as well as its time period.
questions.solution:
Given mass of the particle, $m = 2.0 \times 10^{-10} \text{ g} = 2.0 \times 10^{-13} \text{ kg}$

Charge, $q = 2.0 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C}$

Speed, $v = 2.0 \times 10^3 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Magnetic field, $B = 0.10 \text{ T}$

The radius of the circular path is given by:

$r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$

Substituting the given values:

$r = \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{-13} \times 2.0 \times 10^3}{2.0 \times 10^{-8} \times 0.10}$

$r = \dfrac{4.0 \times 10^{-10}}{2.0 \times 10^{-9}} = 0.2 \text{ m} = 20 \text{ cm}$

The time period of revolution is given by:

$T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB} = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v}$

Substituting the values:

$T = \dfrac{2 \times 3.14 \times 0.2}{2.0 \times 10^3}$

$T = \dfrac{1.256}{2.0 \times 10^3} = 6.28 \times 10^{-4} \text{ s} \approx 6.3 \times 10^{-4} \text{ s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a magnetic field of strength $0.10 \text{ T}$, a proton moves in a circle of radius $1 \text{ cm}$. Determine the radius of the circle traced by an $\alpha$-particle travelling at the same speed within the same magnetic field.
questions.solution:
The radius of a charged particle moving in a uniform magnetic field is given by $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$.

Since the speed $v$ and magnetic field $B$ are the same for both particles, the radius is proportional to the mass-to-charge ratio:

$r \propto \dfrac{m}{q}$

For a proton, let mass be $m$ and charge be $e$. Then $r_{p} \propto \dfrac{m}{e}$.

For an $\alpha$-particle, mass is $4m$ and charge is $2e$. Then $r_{\alpha} \propto \dfrac{4m}{2e} = \dfrac{2m}{e}$.

Taking the ratio of the radii:

$\dfrac{r_{\alpha}}{r_{p}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{2m}{e}}{\dfrac{m}{e}} = 2$

Given $r_{p} = 1 \text{ cm}$, we get:

$r_{\alpha} = 2 \times 1 \text{ cm} = 2 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An electron possessing a kinetic energy of $100 \text{ eV}$ circulates in a path of radius $10 \text{ cm}$ within a magnetic field. Determine the magnetic field and the number of revolutions per second completed by the electron.
questions.solution:
Kinetic energy of the electron, $K = 100 \text{ eV} = 100 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J} = 1.6 \times 10^{-17} \text{ J}$

The radius of the circular path is given by $R = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mK}}{qB}$

Rearranging for magnetic field $B$:

$B = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mK}}{qR}$

Substituting the standard values ($m = 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$, $q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, $R = 0.1 \text{ m}$):

$B = \dfrac{\sqrt{2 \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-17}}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 0.1}$

$B = \dfrac{\sqrt{29.12 \times 10^{-48}}}{1.6 \times 10^{-20}} = \dfrac{5.396 \times 10^{-24}}{1.6 \times 10^{-20}} \approx 3.37 \times 10^{-4} \text{ T}$

The number of revolutions per second is the frequency $f$, given by:

$f = \dfrac{qB}{2\pi m}$

$f = \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 3.37 \times 10^{-4}}{2 \times 3.14 \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31}}$

$f = \dfrac{5.392 \times 10^{-23}}{57.148 \times 10^{-31}} \approx 9.43 \times 10^6 \text{ Hz}$

Rounding off to two significant figures, we get $B = 3.4 \times 10^{-4} \text{ T}$ and $f = 9.4 \times 10^6 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.q: A narrow beam of protons having kinetic energy $K$ emerges from an accelerator. The beam is deflected by a perpendicular magnetic field such that it just misses a plane target kept at a distance $l$ in front of the accelerator. Determine the magnetic field. (Assume $m_p$ and $e$ represent the mass and charge of a proton, respectively).
questions.solution:
The momentum of a proton with kinetic energy $K$ is given by $p = \sqrt{2 m_p K}$.

When the proton beam enters a perpendicular magnetic field $B$, it follows a circular path of radius $R$ given by:

$R = \dfrac{p}{eB} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2 m_p K}}{eB}$

The protons emerge from the accelerator and move towards the plane target. The maximum forward distance traveled by a particle moving in a circular path (starting from the origin and tangent to the initial velocity) is equal to its radius $R$.

For the beam to just miss the plane target kept at a distance $l$ in front of the accelerator, the maximum forward distance must be equal to $l$.

Therefore, $R = l$.

Substituting the value of $R$:

$l = \dfrac{\sqrt{2 m_p K}}{eB}$

Rearranging the above equation to solve for the magnetic field $B$:

$B = \dfrac{\sqrt{2 m_p K}}{e l}$

questions.q: After being accelerated through a potential difference of $12 \text{ kV}$, a charged particle attains a speed of $1.0 \times 10^6 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. It is subsequently injected perpendicularly into a magnetic field of strength $0.2 \text{ T}$. Determine the radius of the circle described by the particle.
questions.solution:
The kinetic energy gained by the charged particle when accelerated through a potential difference $V$ is given by:

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = qV$

$\Rightarrow \dfrac{m}{q} = \dfrac{2V}{v^2}$

When the particle is injected perpendicularly into a magnetic field $B$, the radius $r$ of the circular path is:

$r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$

Substituting the value of $\dfrac{m}{q}$ into the expression for $r$:

$r = \left(\dfrac{2V}{v^2}\right) \dfrac{v}{B} = \dfrac{2V}{vB}$

Given $V = 12 \times 10^3 \text{ V}$, $v = 1.0 \times 10^6 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, and $B = 0.2 \text{ T}$, we get:

$r = \dfrac{2 \times 12 \times 10^3}{1.0 \times 10^6 \times 0.2}$

$r = \dfrac{24 \times 10^3}{2 \times 10^5}$

$r = 12 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m} = 12 \text{ cm}$

questions.q: Determine the acceleration of a proton that is projected perpendicularly into a uniform magnetic field of $0.6 \text{ T}$ with a velocity of $3 \times 10^6 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The magnetic force acting on a charged particle moving in a magnetic field is given by $F = qvB\sin\theta$.

Since the proton is projected perpendicularly, $\theta = 90^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}$, which gives $F = qvB$.

The acceleration of the proton is $a = \dfrac{F}{m} = \dfrac{qvB}{m}$.

Substituting the standard values for a proton ($q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, $m = 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$) and the given values:

$a = \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 3 \times 10^6 \times 0.6}{1.67 \times 10^{-27}}$

$a = \dfrac{2.88 \times 10^{-13}}{1.67 \times 10^{-27}}$

$a \approx 1.72 \times 10^{14} \text{ m s}^{-2}$

questions.q: An electron travels along a circle of radius $1 \text{ m}$ in a perpendicular magnetic field of strength $0.50 \text{ T}$. What would its speed be, and is this speed reasonable?
questions.solution:
The radius of the circular path of a charged particle in a perpendicular magnetic field is given by $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$.

Rearranging for speed $v$, we get $v = \dfrac{qBr}{m}$.

Substituting the given values:

$v = \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 0.50 \times 1}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}}$

$v = \dfrac{0.8 \times 10^{-19}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}} \approx 8.8 \times 10^{10} \text{ m s}^{-1}$

The calculated speed is $8.8 \times 10^{10} \text{ m s}^{-1}$, which is significantly greater than the speed of light in vacuum ($c = 3 \times 10^{8} \text{ m s}^{-1}$).

Since no material particle can travel faster than the speed of light, this speed is unreasonable.

questions.q: A particle of mass $m$ and positive charge $q$ travels with a uniform velocity $v$ and enters a region of magnetic field $B$, as shown in the figure. How much time does the particle spend inside the magnetic field?
questions.solution:
When a particle of mass $m$ and positive charge $q$ enters a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ perpendicular to its velocity, it moves in a circular path with an angular speed $\omega = \dfrac{qB}{m}$.

The magnetic field is directed into the page. Applying the right-hand rule for the magnetic force $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$, the force on the positive charge at the point of entry is directed upwards and to the right. This indicates that the center of the circular path lies outside the magnetic field region.

The particle enters the field at an angle $\theta$ with the normal. Due to the symmetry of the circular path, it will exit the field at the same angle $\theta$ with the normal.

The angle that the velocity vector turns through is equal to the angle subtended by the circular arc at the center. From the geometry of the path, the radii at the entry and exit points each make an angle $\theta$ with the boundary. The angle subtended by the arc at the center is $\phi = \pi - 2\theta$.

The time spent by the particle inside the magnetic field is given by $t = \dfrac{\phi}{\omega}$.

Substituting the values, we get $t = \dfrac{\pi - 2\theta}{\dfrac{qB}{m}} = \dfrac{m}{qB}(\pi - 2\theta)$.

Answer: $\dfrac{m}{q B}(\pi - 2\theta)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of mass $m$ and negative charge of magnitude $q$ travels with a uniform velocity $v$ and enters a region of magnetic field $B$, as shown in the figure. Determine the radius of the arc, the angle subtended by the arc at the centre, and the time the particle stays inside the magnetic field, respectively.
questions.solution:
Let the boundary of the magnetic field be the x-axis and the normal to it be the y-axis. The particle enters the magnetic field at the origin $(0,0)$.

The velocity of the particle makes an angle $\theta$ with the vertical (y-axis). From the figure, the velocity vector is directed downwards and to the right. Thus, the initial velocity is:
$\vec{v} = v\sin\theta \hat{i} - v\cos\theta \hat{j}$

The magnetic field is directed into the page:
$\vec{B} = -B\hat{k}$

The magnetic force on the negatively charged particle is:
$\vec{F} = -q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B}) = -q[(v\sin\theta \hat{i} - v\cos\theta \hat{j}) \times (-B\hat{k})]$
$\vec{F} = -q(-vB\sin\theta (\hat{i} \times \hat{k}) + vB\cos\theta (\hat{j} \times \hat{k}))$
$\vec{F} = -q(vB\sin\theta \hat{j} + vB\cos\theta \hat{i}) = -qvB\cos\theta \hat{i} - qvB\sin\theta \hat{j}$

The force is directed downwards and to the left, which means the center of the circular path lies in the third quadrant relative to the entry point. The particle will curve to the left and trace a major arc before exiting the magnetic field.

The radius of the circular path is given by equating the magnetic force to the centripetal force:
$qvB = \dfrac{mv^2}{R} \implies R = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$

Let $C$ be the center of the circular path, $P$ be the entry point, and $Q$ be the exit point. The boundary $PQ$ is horizontal. The radius $CP$ is perpendicular to the entry velocity $\vec{v}$. Since $\vec{v}$ makes an angle $\theta$ with the vertical, $CP$ makes an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal boundary $PQ$.

By symmetry, the radius $CQ$ also makes an angle $\theta$ with the boundary $PQ$. In the isosceles triangle $CPQ$, the angle subtended by the chord $PQ$ at the center $C$ is:
$\angle PCQ = \pi - (\theta + \theta) = \pi - 2\theta$

Since the center $C$ is below the boundary and the particle travels through the magnetic field region (also below the boundary), the path traced is the major arc of the circle. The angle subtended by this major arc at the center is:
$\text{Angle} = 2\pi - (\pi - 2\theta) = \pi + 2\theta$

The time spent by the particle inside the magnetic field is:
$t = \dfrac{\text{Distance}}{\text{Speed}} = \dfrac{R \times \text{Angle}}{v} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{mv}{qB}\right)(\pi + 2\theta)}{v} = \dfrac{m}{qB}(\pi + 2\theta)$

Answer: $\dfrac{m v}{q B}$, $\pi + 2\theta$, $\dfrac{m}{q B}(\pi + 2\theta)$

questions.q: A particle with mass $m$ and charge $q$ is projected into a region having a perpendicular magnetic field $B$. Determine the angle of deviation of the particle when it exits the magnetic field, if the width $d$ of the region is very slightly smaller than $\dfrac{2mv}{qB}$.
questions.solution:
The radius of the circular path of a charged particle in a perpendicular magnetic field is given by $R = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$.

When the particle enters the magnetic field perpendicularly to its boundary, the maximum horizontal distance it can penetrate into the region is equal to its radius $R$.

The given width of the magnetic field region is $d \approx \dfrac{2mv}{qB} = 2R$.

Since the width of the region $d$ is greater than the maximum penetration depth $R$ ($d > R$), the particle will not be able to cross the magnetic field region. Instead, it will complete a semicircular path inside the magnetic field and exit from the same face it entered.

Determine the isotopes present in the ion beam. Assume the mass of an ion is given by $A(1.6 \times 10^{-27}) \text{ kg}$, where $A$ represents the mass number.
questions.solution:
When a charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field perpendicularly, it moves in a circular path of radius $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$.

The separation between the incident beam and the emergent beam in the backward direction is the diameter of the circular path, $d = 2r = \dfrac{2mv}{qB}$.

Substituting the given values:
$d = \dfrac{2 \times (A \times 1.6 \times 10^{-27}) \times 6.0 \times 10^4}{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 0.5}$

$d = 24 \times 10^{-4} A \text{ m} = 0.24 A \text{ cm}$

For the first beam, $d_1 = 3.0 \text{ cm}$:
$A_1 = \dfrac{3.0}{0.24} = 12.5$

For the second beam, $d_2 = 3.5 \text{ cm}$:
$A_2 = \dfrac{3.5}{0.24} \approx 14.6$

Since the mass number $A$ must be an integer, the closest valid carbon isotopes are $12$ and $14$. Using the standard atomic mass unit $1 \text{ amu} \approx 1.66 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$ instead of the given approximation yields $d \approx 0.25 A \text{ cm}$, which gives exactly $A_1 = 12$ and $A_2 = 14$.

The kinetic energy acquired by an ion accelerated through a potential difference $V$ is $K = qV$.

$B = 20.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ T}$
$q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$
$m = A \times 1.6 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$

$R = \dfrac{1}{20.0 \times 10^{-3}} \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times A \times 1.6 \times 10^{-27} \times 500}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}}}$

$R = 50 \sqrt{A \times 10^{-5}} \text{ m}$

For the isotope with mass number $A = 57$:
$R_{57} = 5 \sqrt{570} \approx 5 \times 23.87 \text{ cm} \approx 119.35 \text{ cm} \approx 119 \text{ cm}$

questions.q: A narrow beam of singly charged potassium ions with a kinetic energy of $32 \text{ keV}$ enters a region of width $1.00 \text{ cm}$ that contains a magnetic field of strength $0.500 \text{ T}$, as shown in the figure. The ions are subsequently collected on a screen located $95.5 \text{ cm}$ away from the magnetic field region. Assuming the beam consists of isotopes with atomic weights $39$ and $41$, determine the separation between the points where these isotopes hit the screen. Use the mass of a potassium ion as $A(1.6 \times 10^{-27}) \text{ kg}$, where $A$ represents the mass number.
questions.solution:
The radius of the circular path of an ion in the magnetic field is given by $R = \dfrac{mv}{qB} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mK}}{qB}$.

Since the width of the magnetic field $d$ is much smaller than $R$, the deflection angle $\theta$ is small. The angle of emergence is $\theta \approx \sin\theta = \dfrac{d}{R}$.

The transverse deflection of the ion inside the magnetic field is $y_1 = R(1 - \cos\theta) \approx R \dfrac{\theta^2}{2} = \dfrac{d^2}{2R}$.

After exiting the magnetic field, the ion travels in a straight line for a distance $L$ to the screen. The additional deflection is $y_2 = L \tan\theta \approx L\theta = \dfrac{Ld}{R}$.

The total deflection on the screen is $y = y_1 + y_2 = \dfrac{d^2}{2R} + \dfrac{Ld}{R} = \dfrac{d}{R}\left(L + \dfrac{d}{2}\right)$.

Let $D = L + \dfrac{d}{2} = 95.5 \text{ cm} + 0.5 \text{ cm} = 96.0 \text{ cm} = 0.96 \text{ m}$.

Substituting $R$, we get $y = \dfrac{d D q B}{\sqrt{2mK}}$.

The mass of the ion is $m = A m_0$, where $m_0 = 1.6 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$ and $A$ is the mass number.

The separation between the two isotopes on the screen is $\Delta y = y_{39} - y_{41} = \dfrac{d D q B}{\sqrt{2 m_0 K}} \left( \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{39}} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{41}} \right)$.

Let's calculate the constant factor:
$d = 0.01 \text{ m}$
$D = 0.96 \text{ m}$
$q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$
$B = 0.500 \text{ T}$
$K = 32 \text{ keV} = 32 \times 10^3 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$
$2 m_0 K = 2 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-27}) \times (32 \times 10^3 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}) = 16.384 \times 10^{-42} \text{ kg}^2 \text{ m}^2 / \text{ s}^2$
$\sqrt{2 m_0 K} = \sqrt{16.384 \times 10^{-42}} \approx 4.048 \times 10^{-21} \text{ kg m/s}$

Now, substituting the values:
$\dfrac{d D q B}{\sqrt{2 m_0 K}} = \dfrac{0.01 \times 0.96 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 0.5}{4.048 \times 10^{-21}} = \dfrac{0.768 \times 10^{-21}}{4.048 \times 10^{-21}} \approx 0.1897 \text{ m}$

The difference in the mass factor is:
$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{39}} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{41}} \approx 0.16013 - 0.15617 = 0.00396$

Thus, the separation is:
$\Delta y \approx 0.1897 \times 0.00396 \approx 0.00075 \text{ m} = 0.75 \text{ mm}$.

Answer: $0.75 \text{ mm}$

questions.q: As illustrated in the figure, a convex lens of focal length $12 ext{ cm}$ is situated within a uniform magnetic field $B$ of magnitude $1.2 ext{ T}$ oriented parallel to its principal axis. A particle with a mass of $2.0 imes 10^{-5} ext{ kg}$ and a charge of $2.0 imes 10^{-3} ext{ C}$ is projected perpendicular to the plane of the diagram at a speed of $4.8 ext{ m s}^{-1}$. The particle travels along a circular path whose centre lies on the principal axis, $18 ext{ cm}$ from the lens. Determine the radius of the circle along which the image of the particle moves.
questions.solution:
The radius of the circular path of the charged particle in the magnetic field is given by:
$R = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$

Substituting the given values:
$R = \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{-5} \times 4.8}{2.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 1.2} = \dfrac{9.6 \times 10^{-5}}{2.4 \times 10^{-3}} = 4 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m} = 4 \text{ cm}$

The circular path of the particle acts as an object for the convex lens. The plane of this circle is perpendicular to the principal axis.
Given the object distance $u = -18 \text{ cm}$ and the focal length of the convex lens $f = +12 \text{ cm}$.

Using the lens formula:
$\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$
$\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{-18} = \dfrac{1}{12}$
$\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{18} = \dfrac{1}{12}$
$\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{12} - \dfrac{1}{18} = \dfrac{3 - 2}{36} = \dfrac{1}{36}$
$v = 36 \text{ cm}$

The transverse magnification $m$ is:
$m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{36}{-18} = -2$

The radius of the circle along which the image moves is:
$R' = |m| \times R = |-2| \times 4 \text{ cm} = 8 \text{ cm}$

questions.q: From an electron gun, electrons are emitted with negligible speed and subsequently accelerated along the $x$-axis by a potential difference $V$. Emerging from a narrow hole, these electrons enter a uniform magnetic field $B$ that points along the same axis. A fraction of the electrons exiting the hole do so at slightly divergent angles, as shown in the figure. Determine the distance along the $x$-axis at which these paraxial electrons are refocussed.
questions.solution:
The kinetic energy of the electron after being accelerated by a potential difference $V$ is given by:

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = eV \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2eV}{m}}$

The electrons enter the magnetic field at a small angle $\theta$ (since they are paraxial) with the $x$-axis. The velocity component parallel to the magnetic field is:

$v_{\parallel} = v \cos\theta \approx v$

The time period of one revolution in the uniform magnetic field is independent of the velocity and is given by:

$T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{eB}$

The electrons will refocus on the $x$-axis after completing one full revolution. The distance along the $x$-axis at which they refocus is the pitch of their helical path:

$x = v_{\parallel} T \approx v T$

Substituting the expressions for $v$ and $T$:

$x = \sqrt{\dfrac{2eV}{m}} \times \dfrac{2\pi m}{eB}$

$x = \sqrt{\dfrac{2eV}{m} \times \dfrac{4\pi^2 m^2}{e^2 B^2}}$

$x = \sqrt{\dfrac{8\pi^2 m V}{e B^2}}$

questions.q: Consider two particles, each of mass $m$, positioned at a separation distance $d$ inside a uniform magnetic field $B$. The particles possess opposite charges of equal magnitude $q$. At an initial time $t = 0$, they are projected directly towards one another, each travelling with a speed $v$. Assume that the Coulomb interaction between the charges is turned off. Let $v_m$ denote the maximum projection speed that allows the particles to avoid a collision. Suppose the particles are projected with a speed $v = 2 v_m$ and undergo a completely inelastic collision. How will the combined mass move following the collision?
options: It moves with a constant speed $2 v_m$ along a straight line drawn upward in the plane of the figure through the point of collision.
It moves in a circular path of radius $d$ with a constant speed $v_m$.
It moves with a constant speed $v_m$ along a straight line drawn upward in the plane of the figure through the point of collision.
It comes to rest immediately at the point of collision.
questions.solution:
The magnetic force on a moving charge is given by $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$. For the particle with charge $q$ moving with velocity $v\hat{i}$ in a magnetic field $-B\hat{k}$, the force is $qvB\hat{j}$ (upwards). For the particle with charge $-q$ moving with velocity $-v\hat{i}$, the force is also $qvB\hat{j}$ (upwards). Thus, both particles move in circular paths curving upwards.

The radius of the circular path is $R = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$.

To just avoid collision, the two circular paths must be tangent to each other. Since the initial separation is $d$, the sum of their radii must be equal to $d$.

$2R_m = d \Rightarrow R_m = \dfrac{d}{2}$

The maximum speed to avoid collision is $v_m = \dfrac{qBR_m}{m} = \dfrac{qBd}{2m}$.

When the particles are projected with speed $v = 2v_m$, the new radius of their paths is $R = \dfrac{m(2v_m)}{qB} = 2R_m = d$.

Let the collision occur after the velocity vectors have rotated by an angle $\theta$. The horizontal distance covered by each particle is $\dfrac{d}{2}$.

From the geometry of the circular path, the horizontal displacement is $R \sin\theta$.

$R \sin\theta = \dfrac{d}{2}$

Substituting $R = d$, we get $\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \theta = 30^{\circ}$.

The velocities of the particles just before the collision are:

$\vec{v}_1 = v \cos(30^{\circ})\hat{i} + v \sin(30^{\circ})\hat{j}$

$\vec{v}_2 = -v \cos(30^{\circ})\hat{i} + v \sin(30^{\circ})\hat{j}$

Since the collision is completely inelastic, the particles stick together. By conservation of linear momentum:

$m\vec{v}_1 + m\vec{v}_2 = (2m)\vec{v}_f$

$\vec{v}_f = \dfrac{\vec{v}_1 + \vec{v}_2}{2} = v \sin(30^{\circ})\hat{j} = \dfrac{v}{2}\hat{j}$

Given $v = 2v_m$, the final velocity is $\vec{v}_f = v_m\hat{j}$.

The combined mass has a net charge of $q + (-q) = 0$. Therefore, it experiences no magnetic force and moves with a constant speed $v_m$ along a straight line drawn upward.

Answer: It moves with a constant speed $v_m$ along a straight line drawn upward in the plane of the figure through the point of collision.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform magnetic field of magnitude $0.20 \text{ T}$ is directed from east to west in space. At what speed must a particle of mass $0.010 \text{ g}$ and charge $1.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ C}$ be projected from south to north in order to travel with a uniform velocity?
questions.solution:
Let the directions be represented by unit vectors: East as $\hat{i}$, North as $\hat{j}$, and vertically upward as $\hat{k}$.

The magnetic field is directed from East to West, so $\vec{B} = -B \hat{i}$.

The particle is projected from South to North, so its velocity is $\vec{v} = v \hat{j}$.

The magnetic force on the particle is $\vec{F}_m = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B}) = q(v \hat{j} \times (-B \hat{i})) = qvB \hat{k}$.

The magnetic force acts vertically upwards. For the particle to travel with uniform velocity, the net force must be zero. Thus, the upward magnetic force must balance the downward gravitational force:

$qvB = mg$

Substituting the given values $m = 0.010 \text{ g} = 1.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ kg}$, $q = 1.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ C}$, $B = 0.20 \text{ T}$, and $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$v = \dfrac{mg}{qB} = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-5} \times 9.8}{1.0 \times 10^{-5} \times 0.20}$

$v = \dfrac{9.8}{0.20} = 49 \text{ m/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle travels in a circle of diameter $1.0 \text{ cm}$ under the influence of a $0.40 \text{ T}$ magnetic field. The application of a $200 \text{ V m}^{-1}$ electric field makes the path straight. Determine the charge-to-mass ratio of the particle.
questions.solution:
When the path of the particle is straight under the combined electric and magnetic fields, the electric force balances the magnetic force.

$qE = qvB \Rightarrow v = \dfrac{E}{B}$

Substituting the given values $E = 200 \text{ V m}^{-1}$ and $B = 0.40 \text{ T}$:

$v = \dfrac{200}{0.40} = 500 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

When the particle travels in a circle under the influence of the magnetic field alone, the radius of the circular path is given by:

$r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$

Rearranging for the charge-to-mass ratio:

$\dfrac{q}{m} = \dfrac{v}{rB}$

The diameter of the circle is $1.0 \text{ cm}$, so the radius is $r = 0.5 \text{ cm} = 5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$.

Substituting the values of $v$, $r$, and $B$:

$\dfrac{q}{m} = \dfrac{500}{5 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.40}$

$\dfrac{q}{m} = \dfrac{500}{2 \times 10^{-3}} = 2.5 \times 10^5 \text{ C kg}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Travelling at a speed of $2.0 \times 10^5 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, a proton passes undeflected through crossed electric and magnetic fields that are perpendicular to each other. The proton's velocity is perpendicular to both fields. After the electric field is switched off, the proton travels in a circle of radius $4.0 \text{ cm}$. Determine the magnitudes of the electric and magnetic fields. Assume the mass of the proton is $1.6 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$.
questions.solution:
When the proton moves undeflected in crossed electric and magnetic fields, the electric force balances the magnetic force:

$qE = qvB \Rightarrow E = vB$

When the electric field is switched off, the proton moves in a circular path under the influence of the magnetic field. The radius of the circular path is given by:

$r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$

Rearranging for the magnetic field $B$:

$B = \dfrac{mv}{qr}$

Substituting the given values ($m = 1.6 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$, $v = 2.0 \times 10^5 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, $q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, $r = 4.0 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$):

$B = \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{-27} \times 2.0 \times 10^5}{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 4.0 \times 10^{-2}}$

$B = \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{-22}}{4.0 \times 10^{-21}} = 0.05 \text{ T}$

Now, substituting $B$ to find the electric field $E$:

$E = vB = (2.0 \times 10^5) \times 0.05$

$E = 1.0 \times 10^4 \text{ N C}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle with a mass of $5.0 \times 10^{-12} \text{ kg}$ and a charge of $5.0 \mu\text{C}$ is projected at a speed of $1.0 \text{ km s}^{-1}$ into a magnetic field of magnitude $5.0 \text{ mT}$. The angle between the velocity and the magnetic field is $\sin^{-1}(0.90)$. Determine the diameter of the resulting helical path and its pitch.
questions.solution:
Given:
Mass $m = 5.0 \times 10^{-12} \text{ kg}$
Charge $q = 5.0 \mu\text{C} = 5.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$
Speed $v = 1.0 \text{ km s}^{-1} = 1.0 \times 10^3 \text{ m s}^{-1}$
Magnetic field $B = 5.0 \text{ mT} = 5.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ T}$
Angle $\theta = \sin^{-1}(0.90) \Rightarrow \sin\theta = 0.90$

From trigonometric identity, $\cos\theta = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2\theta} = \sqrt{1 - 0.90^2} = \sqrt{0.19} \approx 0.436$

The radius of the helical path is given by:
$r = \dfrac{mv\sin\theta}{qB}$

Substituting the values:
$r = \dfrac{5.0 \times 10^{-12} \times 1.0 \times 10^3 \times 0.90}{5.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 5.0 \times 10^{-3}}$

$r = \dfrac{4.5 \times 10^{-9}}{25.0 \times 10^{-9}} = 0.18 \text{ m} = 18 \text{ cm}$

The diameter of the helical path is:
$D = 2r = 2 \times 18 \text{ cm} = 36 \text{ cm}$

The pitch of the helical path is given by:
$p = v\cos\theta \times T = v\cos\theta \times \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$

Substituting the values:
$p = 1.0 \times 10^3 \times \sqrt{0.19} \times \dfrac{2\pi \times 5.0 \times 10^{-12}}{5.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 5.0 \times 10^{-3}}$

$p = 436 \times \dfrac{10\pi \times 10^{-12}}{25.0 \times 10^{-9}} = 436 \times 0.4\pi \times 10^{-3} \approx 0.548 \text{ m}$

$p \approx 54.8 \text{ cm} \approx 55 \text{ cm}$

Charge of proton $q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$

The radius of the helical path is given by:
$r = \dfrac{m v_{\perp}}{q B}$

Solving for the perpendicular velocity component $v_{\perp}$:
$v_{\perp} = \dfrac{q B r}{m} = \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 0.020 \times 0.05}{1.6 \times 10^{-27}} = 1.0 \times 10^5 \text{ m/s}$

The pitch of the helical path is given by:
$p = v_{\parallel} T = v_{\parallel} \left( $\dfrac{2 \pi m}{q B} \right)

Solving for the parallel velocity component $v_{\parallel}$:
$v_{\parallel} = $\dfrac{p q B}{2 \pi m} = \dfrac{0.20 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 0.020}{2 \pi \times 1.6 \times 10^{-27}}

$v_{\parallel} = $\dfrac{0.004}{2 \pi} \times$10^8 = $\dfrac{2}{\pi} \times$10^5 \approx 6.4 \times 10^4 \text{ m/s}$

Thus, the parallel and perpendicular velocity components are $6.4 \times 10^4 \text{ m/s}$ and $1.0 \times 10^5 \text{ m/s}$ respectively.

questions.q: A particle with mass $m$ and charge $q$ is released from the origin in a region where the electric field and magnetic field are given as $\vec{B} = -B_0 \vec{j}$ and $\vec{E} = E_0 \vec{k}$. Determine the particle's speed as a function of its $z$-coordinate.
questions.solution:
By the work-energy theorem, the total work done on the particle is equal to its change in kinetic energy.

The magnetic force $\vec{F}_m = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$ is always perpendicular to the velocity vector, so the work done by the magnetic field is zero.

The electric force acting on the particle is $\vec{F}_e = q\vec{E} = q E_0 \hat{k}$. The work done by the electric field when the particle undergoes a displacement from the origin to a position with $z$-coordinate $z$ is $W_e = q E_0 z$.

Equating the total work done to the change in kinetic energy:

$W_e + W_m = \Delta K$

$q E_0 z + 0 = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2$

$v^2 = \dfrac{2 q E_0 z}{m}$

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 q E_0 z}{m}}$

questions.q: From the negative plate of a parallel plate capacitor charged to a potential difference $V$, an electron is emitted with negligible speed. The separation between the plates is $d$, and a magnetic field $B$ exists in the space as shown in the figure. Which of the following conditions ensures that the electron will fail to strike the upper plate?
questions.solution:
Let the lower plate be at $y = 0$ and the upper plate be at $y = d$.

The electric field between the plates is $E = \dfrac{V}{d}$, directed downwards.

The magnetic field is $\vec{B} = B \hat{k}$.

The equations of motion for the electron are given by the Lorentz force:

$m_e \dfrac{d\vec{v}}{dt} = -e(\vec{E} + \vec{v} \times \vec{B})$

Considering the x-component of the force:

$m_e \dfrac{dv_x}{dt} = -e B v_y = -e B \dfrac{dy}{dt}$

Integrating with respect to time and using the initial condition $v_x = 0$ at $y = 0$:

$m_e v_x = -e B y \Rightarrow v_x = -\dfrac{e B}{m_e} y$

By the work-energy theorem, the kinetic energy of the electron at height $y$ is equal to the work done by the electric field:

$\dfrac{1}{2} m_e (v_x^2 + v_y^2) = e E y$

Substituting the expression for $v_x$:

$\dfrac{1}{2} m_e \left( \left(-\dfrac{e B}{m_e} y\right)^2 + v_y^2 \right) = e E y$

At the maximum height $y_{max}$, the vertical component of velocity becomes zero ($v_y = 0$):

$\dfrac{1}{2} m_e \left( \dfrac{e^2 B^2}{m_e^2} y_{max}^2 \right) = e E y_{max}$

$y_{max} = \dfrac{2 m_e E}{e B^2}$

Substituting $E = \dfrac{V}{d}$:

$y_{max} = \dfrac{2 m_e V}{e B^2 d}$

For the electron to fail to strike the upper plate, its maximum height must be strictly less than the plate separation $d$:

$y_{max} < d$

$\dfrac{2 m_e V}{e B^2 d} < d$

$d^2 > \dfrac{2 m_e V}{e B^2}$

$d > \left( \dfrac{2 m_e V}{e B^2} \right)^{1/2}$

Answer: $d > \left(\dfrac{2 m_e V}{e B^2}\right)^{1/2}$
